Whats up guys,

So, a couple of weeks ago I released a video about investing in the Big Six Canadian Banks.

When it comes to “Financial” Stocks, or the Financial sector, many people automatically think of Banks. But there is a segment of the Financial sector that doesn't get the same amount of attention or notoriety. These companies usually fly under the radar…

Yes I'm talking about Life Insurance Companies, or Lifeco’s. The reality is that these companies are old, big, and lucrative just like big banks. In addition, they tend to be fairly stable because much of their revenue comes from insurance premiums which are long term and stable contracts.


When it comes to Canada there are 3 big players that dominate the entire industry. If you're Canadian I'm sure you've heard of them.  Number 1 is Manulife, Number 2 is Sunlife and number 3 is Great West Life, which recently consolidated all their brands to one name: Canada Life. 

Great West Life BTW is owned primarily by the Power Corporation of Canada, a huge Canadian Asset management company which also owns Investors group and Wealth Simple. 

Cool chart you can display:
https://www.powercorporation.com/en/companies/organization-chart/

What about in the U.S. Well some big players include Metlife, which has that iconic NYC building you've probably seen in a bunch of movies as well as Lincoln National, Prudential Financial and a couple of others. 

So how do these companies make money? Well it's no surprise that Life insurance products are their  bread and butter, But don’t think that's their only source of revenue….I did some research on this and these are some of the insurance products these companies offer.

Also don't think these companies only offer insurance products , they also manage Group and Retirement benefits for Corporations. I work at Air Canada for example and Manulife handles our Retirement benefits, which mean you are obliged to buy into Manulife owned Mutual funds.

So in addition to those insurance products, they also offer Investment services to individuals and Businesses alike which means they do Wealth and Asset management.

Also, selling insurance isn't restricted to North America. Manulife and Sunlife for example have growing revenues from Asian markets 

I think you get my point, these are not mom and pop companies here. If we actually look at how long they've been in business, you realize they can be just as old as Banks. Manulife 1887, Sunlife 1865, Great West Life 1847. Metlife, 1868. Etc.


They've been in the game a really long time and know exactly how to price their insurance policies because of the research and data they've accumulated over the years, which simply means, they will always be profitable. Think of them like a Casino, yes there will always be a lucky one time winner but all that money people lose will always balance out the rare winners. Hence the famous expression  “the house always wins”



So what kind of dividends to these companies offer us passive income investors?

Lets check out the current Dividend Yields and the 5 year Dividend History of Manulife and Sunlife real quick, so you can see what buying the individual stocks can give you
.
So the average dividend Yield right now if you invested in big 3 Canadian Lifecos is a little under 6%. Not bad at all considering they consistently increase their dividends. Note that all 3 companies are discounted right now as they have not fully recovered from the COVID market crash, making their dividend yields higher than normal.


So yes investing in the stocks individually can be a good choice. BUT is there a more efficient way to invest in these Life Insurance Companies?

Is there a way to lower your risk and diversify better by getting a piece of not only the Canadian Giants but the U.S. Giants as well?

Lastly and more importantly. Is there a way to get more income than owning the stocks individually?

The answer is Yes to all those questions  and once again, an ETF is the answer.

After looking around, I finally found an amazing ETF from CI First Asset that not only includes the top Lifecos in North America, but also gives a huge 11% dividend. Don't believe me? Let me show you…

comments.text: Hi Adrian. I went back to re-watch your vid on covered call ETF's after watching this one and have a question: Do the managers of these covered call ETF's sell options for the stocks in the ETF's every 30 days? Is there somewhere you can find the dates when the new options are sold for each stock in an ETF? I'm wondering as the stock market recovers if we can expect the dividends of covered call ETF's to decrease because the options are being exercised as the stock price moves up? Thanks!
comments.author: @DL-bl6qp

comments.text:
Hey. 
Dividends will not reduce. What could happen is that the covered call option will be exercised and in that case the owner (us) will make money from that too. The only trade off here for the owner is the potential upside of a bullish market. However we are experiencing a recovering market so it's the best time for the covered Calls ETF. I don't know the exact dates but the main reason why these covered Calls are good for the owners during up and down market, meaning the owner always wins is because of the time elapse factor. The closer it's gets to the date the options expires, the volitlity of the market helps the sale of the option but not the exercise of  it. Bottom line if you buy and hold these covered call ETFs, you get more income and a very well managed ETF for growth
